title: Encapsulation and Access Modifiers
description: Learn how to protect class internals using access modifiers, properties, and data-hiding techniques.

data.text: Encapsulation is the OOP principle of bundling data with the methods that operate on that data, while restricting direct access to some of the object's internal components. Think of it like a car's engine: you use the steering wheel and pedals (public interface) without needing to understand the internal combustion process (hidden implementation).

Without encapsulation, any code could freely modify an object's data, leading to invalid states and hard-to-debug issues. With encapsulation, you enforce rules through a controlled public interface, making your code safer, more maintainable, and easier to test.

data.title: Why It Matters
data.text: Encapsulation prevents external code from putting your object into an invalid state. For example, a BankAccount balance should never be negative — only the Deposit/Withdraw methods should be allowed to change it.

terms.definition: Bundling data and methods together while hiding internal implementation details from outside code.
A keyword (public, private, protected, internal) that controls where a class member can be accessed from.
The code block in a property that runs when the property's value is read.
The code block in a property that runs when the property's value is assigned.
A private field that stores the actual data behind a property.

data.text: C# provides several access modifiers that control the visibility of classes and their members. Understanding when and where to use each is fundamental to writing well-encapsulated code.

rows: Public API — constructors, properties, methods meant for external callers
Internal fields and helper methods that should never be exposed
Members intended for reuse in subclasses via inheritance
Implementation details shared across files in the same project
Members safe for subclassing anywhere OR internal sharing
Same class AND derived classes, same assembly only
Members only accessible to derived classes in the same assembly

data.text: Properties in C# are the preferred way to expose data while maintaining encapsulation. A property looks like a field from the outside but acts like a method internally — the `get` accessor returns the value and the `set` accessor assigns it. You can validate, transform, or log every change through the setter.

data.title: Full Encapsulation with Properties
data.content: A BankAccount class that completely hides its balance field and controls all modifications through methods and properties.

data.text: Notice how `Balance` has a `public get` but a `private set`. External code can check the balance but cannot directly set it — it must use `Deposit()` or `Withdraw()`. This is the essence of encapsulation: control the mutation of state.

C# offers several property patterns for different scenarios. Auto-properties are the simplest. Full properties with backing fields give you full control. Expression-bodied properties compute values on demand. Init-only setters allow setting a value only during object initialization.

data.title: Property Patterns
data.content: Auto-properties, init-only, computed, and full properties with backing fields.

data.text: A key benefit of encapsulation is enforcing business rules at the point of data entry. Rather than trusting callers to provide valid data, the class validates internally. This prevents invalid object states that can cause bugs elsewhere in the application.

data.title: Validation in Setters
data.content: Using property setters to enforce business rules and keep object state valid.

data.title: Anti-patterns to Avoid
items: Making fields public — always use properties instead.
Exposing mutable collections directly — return a copy or use ReadOnlyCollection<T>.
Using empty getters/setters that add no value — either fully expose or fully encapsulate.
Doing heavy work in property getters — properties should be lightweight.
Mixing public and private logic in the same method — keep methods focused.

data.title: Exercise: Encapsulate a Temperature Class
data.description: Create a Temperature class that stores Celsius privately. Expose a public Celsius property with validation (range: -273.15 to double.MaxValue) and a Fahrenheit property that converts to and from Celsius. Throw ArgumentOutOfRangeException for invalid values.
steps: Create a public double Celsius property with validation in the setter.
Create a public double Fahrenheit property that converts to/from Celsius.
Test with values like 0, 100, and -300 (the last one should throw).
data.expectedOutcome: A Temperature object that safely converts between Celsius and Fahrenheit and rejects invalid temperatures.

cards.title: Public Field
cards.description: A publicly accessible variable directly on the class.

cards.title: Public Property
cards.description: A get/set accessor pair that controls access to private data.
pros: Can change backing storage without breaking API

items.question: Why not just make all fields public?
items.answer: Public fields expose internal state directly with no validation or control. Once a field is public, any code can set it to any value, potentially corrupting the object's state. Properties let you validate and maintain invariants.

items.question: What is an init-only setter?
items.answer: An init accessor (public string Name { get; init; }) allows the property to be set only during object initialization (e.g., in a constructor or object initializer). After that, it becomes effectively read-only.

items.question: Should I always make fields private?
items.answer: Yes, as a general rule. Private fields force all access through methods and properties, which gives you a single point to add logging, validation, or change the internal representation later.

items.question: What does private protected mean?
items.answer: private protected restricts access to members of the same class AND derived classes, but only within the same assembly. It combines the restrictions of both private and protected.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Encapsulation hides implementation details behind a controlled public interface.
Access modifiers (public, private, protected, internal) control visibility.
Properties are the primary mechanism for encapsulation in C#.
Validate data in setters to maintain object invariants.
Private backing fields with public properties is the standard pattern.
data.takeaway: Encapsulation is the first pillar of OOP and the foundation of writing maintainable, bug-resistant C# code.
